title: Irenaeus (c. 180)
hook: the glory of God is a human being fully alive

segments.voice: Yesterday, Blandina of Lyon, whose short answer, Christianē eimi, outlasted her torturers. Your line was Christian, I am.

An old friend has drifted into strange teachings, and a bishop writes to call him back. To make his point, he reaches for a memory. When I was a boy, he says, I heard Polycarp. I can still tell you the place where he sat to teach, how he came and went, how he talked about John and the others who had seen the Lord. The bishop is Irenaeus, and Eusebius kept the letter. After the martyrs of Lyon, the church there needs a new bishop. It gets this man, who carries Polycarp's voice in his head.
screen: `A LETTER TO AN OLD FRIEND.` → `I HEARD POLYCARP.` → `A NEW BISHOP FOR LYON.`

segments.voice: Irenaeus wrote a long work that came to be called Against Heresies. First, what he was up against. Some teachers of his day said the material world was a mistake, made by a lesser power. The body was a cage. Salvation was secret knowledge, handed to a few who were in on it. Second, his answer. One God, he says, made heaven and earth, and made them good. The same God formed the human being from the earth, and the Son of God took real flesh. So the body isn't a prison to escape. It's part of what God is saving. Third, the line. In the Latin text it begins: Gloria enim Dei vivens homo. For the glory of God is a living human being. The Catechism of the Catholic Church gives it this way: the glory of God is man fully alive. That's today's line. Fourth, the second half. The sentence keeps going: and the life of a human being is the vision of God. Fully alive, for Irenaeus, isn't the same as busy, or impressive, or happy all the time. It's a life turned toward God, seeing God, and made more human by it, not less. A God glorified by people being small and miserable wasn't the God Irenaeus knew. And notice when he wrote it. Lyon had just lost its martyrs. Irenaeus didn't pretend life was easy. Yet he wrote that God's glory looks like a person coming fully alive.
screen: `AGAINST THE SECRET TEACHERS.` · `ONE GOD MADE IT ALL GOOD.` · `GLORIA DEI VIVENS HOMO.` · `LIFE IS SEEING GOD.` · then, large: `FULLY ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Feel your body for a moment: your feet, your hands, the air coming in, part of the good world, Irenaeus says, not a cage. Then pick one ordinary thing ahead of you today, a meal, a walk, a conversation, washing a pan, and picture doing it with all of you there, no scrolling, no half-listening. If you pray, offer that one thing to God before you begin.
Irenaeus. The bishop of Lyon who heard Polycarp as a boy and said the glory of God is a human being fully alive. Today's word.
Your line: fully alive. Not busier or more impressive, just more human. That's day seven hundred nine.

howItsDone: Catholics honor Saint Irenaeus as a bishop and Doctor of the Church, and his line on the glory of God is quoted in the Catechism of the Catholic Church in its teaching on creation.

fork.setup: you're the new bishop of Lyon. teachers are saying the world is a mistake and only secret knowledge saves. what do you do?
options: stay quiet and let it pass.
write a long answer: one God made it all good.
start a secret circle of your own.
fork.reveal: Irenaeus wrote Against Heresies, insisting one God made heaven and earth, and that the flesh is part of what God saves.

chat.says: What did Irenaeus mean, the glory of God is a person fully alive?
options: A life turned toward God, seeing God, and made more human by it, body and all.
Being busy and successful, since a full calendar shows how alive you are.
Being happy all the time, since any sadness means you've drifted from God.
chat.meaning: For Irenaeus, the glory of God is a living human being, and that life is the vision of God: not busy or impressive, but more human.

Irenaeus.meaning: the bishop of Lyon who heard Polycarp as a boy

Polycarp.meaning: the old bishop of Smyrna Irenaeus heard teach

sources.ref: Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1 (summary of the teachings he opposes); 3–5 (one God, creation, the flesh)
Irenaeus, Letter to Florinus, in Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 5.20

notes: Latin of Against Heresies 4.20.7 'Gloria enim Dei vivens homo, vita autem hominis visio Dei': confirm. The English 'a living human being' is the script's plain rendering; CCC 294 has 'the glory of God is man fully alive; moreover man's life is the vision of God' (paraphrased, not quoted).
Letter to Florinus (Eusebius HE 5.20) paraphrased: Irenaeus as a boy heard Polycarp, remembers where he sat, his comings and goings, how he spoke of John and others who had seen the Lord. Confirm.
Irenaeus succeeding Pothinus as bishop of Lyon after the martyrdoms: Eusebius HE 5.5. Confirm.
The summary of the teachings Irenaeus opposed is kept general ('some teachers'); a scholar may prefer naming Valentinians or gnostics.
howItsDone says Irenaeus is a Doctor of the Church (declared by Pope Francis): confirm before release.

Editor: 'Lyon had just buried its martyrs' to 'lost': the letter in Eusebius HE 5.1 says their bodies were burned and thrown into the Rhone, not buried; stock 'the half people forget' to 'the second half'.
Editor 2: review's 'the same short answer' to 'one short answer', matching day 708's edit.

Audit (y3 auditor): 'He said, after all that,' cut: it implied the line was written as an answer to the Lyon martyrdoms, which Against Heresies 4.20.7 does not say. Rest checked against AH 4.20.7, CCC 294, Eusebius HE 5.5 and 5.20; Doctor of the Church (Pope Francis, 2022) correct.
